## Your Organization

**Mercy Ridge Family Clinic** is a federally qualified health center serving a low-income neighborhood on Indianapolis's east side. It sees about 9,000 patients a year — many uninsured or on Medicaid — offering primary care, behavioral health services, dental, and pharmacy all under one roof. The clinic has 85 employees: 12 physicians and nurse practitioners, 8 behavioral health counselors, 10 dental staff, 15 medical assistants, a pharmacy team, and about 30 administrative and support staff.

The clinic is governed by a board of directors that is majority patients — a requirement for federally qualified health centers. In theory, this means the people the clinic serves have real power over its direction. In practice, board meetings are attended by a small number of highly engaged patients, and most staff don't interact with the board at all.

Internally, the clinic has a sharp status hierarchy that tracks clinical credentials. Physicians have significant autonomy over how they practice — they set their own visit formats, make their own referral decisions, and are rarely questioned by administration. Nurse practitioners have less autonomy; their treatment plans are technically subject to physician oversight, though in practice that oversight is often perfunctory. Medical assistants have very little — their work is tightly scripted by protocols, and deviating from those protocols requires escalating to a clinician.

The clinic recently brought in a new executive director who is pushing for a more "team-based care" model: regular interdisciplinary huddles, shared care plans, and medical assistants playing a larger role in patient outreach. Some of the physicians are resistant. One said, privately, that "we went to medical school for a reason." Several medical assistants, meanwhile, say they often know things about patients — family situations, medication challenges, barriers to follow-up — that never make it into the chart because nobody asks them.

The clinic struggles with burnout and turnover, especially among support staff.
